B: Hello. Can you hear me?
A: Yeah, hiya. Rob.
B: Neil. Good to meet you. I have to say, I noticed the OS map behind you in your photo. Dark Peak?
A: Yeah, OL1. It's been up there so long it's gone a bit yellow.
B: I've got the same one, in a drawer. Do you walk out there much?
A: Most weekends I can. I'm in Stockport, so it's easy, train out to Edale or Hayfield. Kinder, Bleaklow, the usual.
B: Bleaklow in the mist is something else. I got properly turned round up there once, years ago, and I'm someone who plans routes on a spreadsheet.
A: Everyone does on Bleaklow. It all looks the same, just groughs and peat.
B: Exactly that. I'm planning the Cromford Canal at the moment, which is rather more civilised. Flat, for one thing.
A: Oh, that's a good one. There's a few water voles round there, apparently, if you're lucky. I've not seen one myself.
B: I'll keep an eye out. You'd know, I suppose. Are you a birder, with the binoculars?
A: Yeah, birds and bats mostly. I'm doing an ecology degree at Man Met. Mature student, second year.
B: Oh, good for you. What were you doing before?
A: Admin at the council. Planning support. Eight years of it. I got bored, so I left. I'd started a degree at eighteen and dropped out after a term, so it sort of felt like unfinished business, really.
B: I can understand that. I didn't go at eighteen at all, and I did an Open University history degree in my forties because it bothered me. It took six years of evenings, but I'm very glad I did it.
A: That's proper commitment, that.
B: Or stubbornness. My wife would say stubbornness. Is it hard, going back? Being older than everyone?
A: Erm, a bit. Most of them are nineteen. They're nice, but I'm sort of the one who knows how to use a spreadsheet. And the money's tight. My partner Hannah's covering more than she should, if I'm honest.
B: That's a lot to take on. Hannah, did you say? My daughter's called Hannah.
A: Ha. That's the thing today, isn't it? Everyone's partner seems to have somebody else's name.
B: I'd noticed that. I half wonder if they've done it on purpose, to see if it throws us. I don't suppose you know what the study's actually about?
A: No idea, to be honest. First impressions, I'm guessing. They had us rate the photos.
B: Yes. I did feel slightly bad doing that, scoring people on a picture of their kitchen.
A: Same. I gave everyone a decent mark, mostly.
B: Diplomatic. Can I ask you a bird question, while I've got an expert?
A: Go on, I'll try. Not an expert, mind.
B: There's a small brown bird that keeps coming to my feeder. Bit like a sparrow, but it skulks underneath, never on the feeder itself. Slightly grey round the face.
A: Sounds like a dunnock, I'd say. They do that, shuffle about underneath picking up what the others drop. Grey head, bit streaky on the back?
B: That's it, I think. A dunnock. Well, that's been bothering me for weeks.
